official.title: Non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs for treating symptomatic uncomplicated urinary tract infections in non-pregnant adult women.

row.question_original: I have a simple urinary tract infection. Should I take an anti-inflammatory like ibuprofen instead of antibiotics?

replies:
**Generally, no—ibuprofen should not replace antibiotics for a suspected bacterial UTI.** It may ease pain, but it doesn’t reliably clear the infection. Using an anti-inflammatory alone can prolong symptoms and increase the risk of the infection spreading to your kidneys.

Contact a healthcare professional to confirm whether you need antibiotics. Some mild bladder infections can be managed with a clinician-supervised delayed-antibiotic plan, but that isn’t suitable for everyone. If you’ve already been prescribed antibiotics, take them as directed rather than substituting ibuprofen.

For discomfort while arranging care:
- Acetaminophen/paracetamol may help. Ibuprofen may also help if it’s safe for you, but avoid it if you’re dehydrated, have kidney disease or stomach ulcers, take blood thinners, or are pregnant unless a clinician advises otherwise.
- Drink enough fluids to avoid dehydration; forcing extra water won’t cure the infection.

**Seek prompt medical care** for fever, chills, back or side pain, vomiting, or worsening symptoms. Get medical advice promptly even with mild symptoms if you’re pregnant, male, immunocompromised, or have kidney disease.

Have you been diagnosed or prescribed antibiotics, and do you have any fever or back/side pain?

The evidence shows a trade-off: **starting with ibuprofen lets some people avoid antibiotics, but causes longer-lasting symptoms and a higher risk of kidney infection.** That’s why it generally isn’t recommended as a replacement.

### What the trials found
These studies mainly enrolled **nonpregnant adult women with uncomplicated bladder infections**, without fever or other signs of kidney infection:

| Randomized trial | Main findings |
|---|---|
| **Ibuprofen vs fosfomycin**, 494 women, *BMJ* (2015) | About **two-thirds of the ibuprofen group recovered without antibiotics**, but they had a greater overall symptom burden. Kidney infection occurred in **5 women given ibuprofen versus 1 given antibiotics**. |
| **Ibuprofen vs pivmecillinam**, 383 women, *PLOS Medicine* (2018) | By day 4, **39% were recovered with ibuprofen versus 74% with antibiotics**. Kidney infection occurred in **7 women in the ibuprofen group versus none in the antibiotic group**. |
| **Diclofenac vs norfloxacin**, 253 women, *BMJ* (2017) | Symptoms resolved by day 3 in **54% versus 80%**, respectively. Kidney infection occurred in **6 women receiving diclofenac versus none receiving antibiotics**. |

Importantly, participants could receive **rescue antibiotics** if symptoms persisted or worsened. These weren’t studies of simply leaving an infection untreated indefinitely.

### How to interpret that
- **Some uncomplicated bladder infections resolve on their own.** Recovering while taking ibuprofen doesn’t mean ibuprofen cured the infection.
- **Antibiotics provide faster, more reliable symptom relief and reduce the risk of kidney infection.**
- Kidney infection was uncommon, but the consistent increase across trials matters. Individual trials had relatively few events, so the exact size of that risk is uncertain.
- Antibiotics also have downsides—side effects and antibiotic resistance—which can make a **clinician-supervised delayed prescription** reasonable for selected people with mild symptoms.

**Bottom line:** The evidence supports antibiotics as the usual treatment for a confirmed bacterial bladder infection—not ibuprofen alone. A delayed-antibiotic approach can be discussed if you’re otherwise healthy, nonpregnant, have mild symptoms, and have reliable access to care. Fever, chills, side/back pain, vomiting, or feeling significantly unwell warrant prompt assessment.

Sources: [Gágyor et al., 2015](https://www.bmj.com/content/351/bmj.h6544); [Vik et al., 2018](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pmed.1002569); [Kronenberg et al., 2017](https://www.bmj.com/content/359/bmj.j4784).
